quote: Frage B, ob Frage A durch endl. Anzahl von Operationen entscheidbar
english: Question B: whether question A is decidable by a finite number of operations.
topic: Notes on foundations: whether a question is decidable by finitely many operations, finiteness proofs with and without an upper bound, existence as consistency, and remarks on the spirit of mathematical research.

triage.modern_statement: This is a meta-question about a given mathematical question A: can A be settled by an effective procedure, meaning finitely many mechanical operations? Today we would ask whether the problem (a set of instances or a class of formulas) is decidable, i.e. recursive or computable. The best-known general version is Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem: is there an algorithm that decides, for any first-order formula, whether it is universally valid (or provable)? Hilbert's notebook sentence is too short to show which question A he had in mind, so it can only be identified as this general decidability question.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert stated the 'problem of the decidability of a mathematical question by a finite number of operations' publicly in 'Axiomatisches Denken' (lecture of 11 Sept 1917, Math. Annalen 78, 1918). He turned it into the Entscheidungsproblem in Hilbert–Ackermann (1928). Alonzo Church (1935–36) and Alan Turing (1936, 'On computable numbers') independently answered it in the negative: no such general decision algorithm exists. That answer relies on the Church–Turing thesis.

evidence.claim: In the 1917 lecture 'Axiomatisches Denken', Hilbert asked for a solution to 'das Problem der Entscheidbarkeit einer mathematischen Frage durch eine endliche Anzahl' [von Operationen]. This anticipates the Entscheidungsproblem of Hilbert–Ackermann (1928). The wording is almost the same as the notebook entry.
'Axiomatisches Denken' appeared in Mathematische Annalen 78 (1918), 405–15. It was a lecture to the Swiss Mathematical Society on 11 September 1917.
Church and Turing proved in 1936 that a general decision algorithm is impossible. Church gave a negative answer in 1935–36 (Church's theorem), and Turing did so independently.
Turing summed up his result by saying that 'the Hilbert Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution'.

triage.why: The notebook wording matches Hilbert's published 1917/18 formulation almost word for word. That formulation became the Entscheidungsproblem, which Church and Turing settled negatively in 1936. It is not one of the 23 Paris problems, although Problem 10 (Diophantine equations) asks a related decidability question. The general topic is still very active today as computability theory and the study of which particular problems are decidable. Confidence is medium, not high, because the fragment does not name question A, and it is an inference that the note matches the published problem.
